title: When the Fed Blinks, Gold Listens: A Week of Divided Signals, Sticky Inflation, and the Quiet Resilience of Precious Metals
text:
The world's most powerful central bank just held its ground, but barely.
 
This week, the Federal Reserve voted 9 to 3 to keep rates unchanged, marking the fifth consecutive hold at 3.50%–3.75%. Three dissenting voices called for an immediate hike. The Treasury yield curve twisted in ways not seen in nearly two decades. U.S. GDP growth slipped to 1.5%. PCE inflation held firm at 3.7%. And across the Strait of Hormuz, the geopolitical fault lines that have reshaped global energy markets since February continued to simmer.
 
In the middle of all of it, gold held above $4,000 per ounce.
 
That is not a coincidence. It is a signal.
 
Our latest WiseGold Weekly Pulse breaks down every major macro and market development from the past week, from the Fed's "hawkish hold" and the BoE's divided vote, to the steepening yield curve, the dollar's late-week retreat, and the World Gold Council's Q2 data showing central banks purchased 289 tonnes of gold in a single quarter.

The macro environment did not gradually shift, it snapped.

title: The Week the Data Lied: Oil, Iran, and the Return of the Stagflation Trade
text:
June's inflation report looked like good news. Headline CPI fell to 3.5%, cooler than expected, driven by a sharp drop in energy prices. Markets exhaled. Rate-cut hopes flickered back to life.
 
Then the Strait of Hormuz happened.
 
Within 48 hours of that print, renewed U.S.-Iran military strikes sent crude oil surging more than 9%, erasing the very disinflationary impulse that had just calmed markets. New Fed Chair Kevin Warsh stood before Congress and made one thing unmistakably clear: the central bank has "no tolerance for persistently elevated inflation", and the July 28–29 FOMC meeting is very much live.
 
This week's WiseGold Weekly Pulse cuts through the noise. We cover the full macro and monetary policy landscape, from the Bank of Korea's first rate hike in over three years, to the ECB's September dilemma, to what a stagflationary oil shock means for gold, silver, platinum, and palladium in a world where the paper market and the physical market are telling very different stories.

title: When Ceasefire Breaks and Rates Hold: What the World's Most Turbulent Week Tells Us About Gold, Risk, and the Road Ahead
text:

Simultaneously, the IMF revised global headline inflation upward to 4.7% for 2026, while projecting growth at a modest 3.0%.
 
In the middle of this convergence of pressures, gold held its ground.

title: When the Fed Speaks and Peace Breaks Out: Gold's Week of Reckoning
text:
This week handed markets two seismic shocks in rapid succession, and precious metals absorbed both.
 
On Wednesday, Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh erased every projected 2026 rate cut from the dot plot, signaling that the era of easy money is not merely paused but potentially reversed. By Friday, the United States and Iran had formally signed a ceasefire in Geneva, collapsing the geopolitical risk premium that had been quietly supporting gold, silver, and crude oil since April.
 
The result was a week that tested the conviction of every precious metals investor. Gold retreated from above $4,300 to near $4,165/oz. Silver shed nearly 9% over the period. Platinum and palladium followed in lockstep.
 
Yet beneath the price action, something more instructive was happening. Indian physical buyers, facing a record 15% import duty, had already compressed a $150/oz discount down to just $25/oz in a matter of weeks. Strategic demand does not disappear under pressure. It waits, and then it moves.
